title: Annual Pay Ranges for Physicians, Dentists, Podiatrists, and Optometrists of the Veterans Health Administration (VHA)
summary:
The Department of Veterans Affairs has announced two updates: new pay ranges for many VA clinicians, now including optometrists, and the appointment of the members who will sit on the VA’s Performance Review Board, which evaluates senior leaders.

For clinicians, the VA is updating its pay tables beginning December 28, 2025. Optometrists are now part of the same pay system used for physicians, dentists, and podiatrists, with pay made up of base, market, and performance components. The minimum pay in two major tables is rising to $123,077, and optometry is added to a table that covers primary care and several other specialties. The goal is to better match the labor market, support recruitment and retention, and offer room for career growth. There is still a cap: total annual compensation cannot exceed the President’s salary, though certain incentives don’t count toward that limit.

The VA also named the members of its Performance Review Board, effective October 24, 2025. This group reviews how the department’s senior executives are performing and helps ensure accountability at the top of the organization.

Who benefits? Veterans may see more stable access to care if the VA can hire and keep hard‑to‑recruit specialists, particularly optometrists. Clinicians at the lower end of the ranges could see higher minimum pay, and optometrists gain a clearer path for advancement within the VA system. The VA itself may have more flexibility to compete for talent, which can support program continuity and reduce turnover.

Who might be negatively affected? Higher pay ranges can add budget pressure, which may require tradeoffs elsewhere if funding is tight. Some clinicians may still feel constrained by the overall pay cap, especially in high‑cost markets or highly specialized fields. Private sector providers in communities near VA facilities could face stiffer competition for optometrists and other clinicians. And for staff awaiting raises, the changes don’t take effect until late December, which may delay immediate benefits. As for the Performance Review Board, any shifts in how senior leaders are evaluated could ripple through priorities and management focus, which not everyone will agree with.

Overall, these steps are about tightening alignment with the broader health care market and formalizing oversight, with the intended outcome of more consistent care for veterans and clearer expectations for VA leaders and clinicians.
